newsitem.title: USA: Colonel denies he wrongly claimed U.S. awards.
newsitem.headline: Colonel denies he wrongly claimed U.S. awards.

text.p: A retired army colonel who questioned medals worn by top Navy admiral Jeremy "Mike" Boorda before Boorda killed himself in 1996 denied on Friday that he himself had wrongly claimed military awards.
Television networks reported on Thursday that Army Col. David Hackworth wrongly claimed credit for two of his own military awards.
"I don't understand what all the drumbeat is, but i have not ever worn an award that the United States Army didn't present to me," Hackworth told MSNBC.

Boorda killed himself in May 1996 shortly before he was to meet with Newsweek magazine reporters, including Hackworth, to discuss whether he properly wore valour pins on his Vietnam War service ribbons.
But Hackworth, a consultant to Newsweek, has deleted two of his own military awards from a list published on his home page on the Internet, networks reported.

The much-decorated Army veteran, who retired from the military in 1971, said on Friday that a number of awards had been "belatedly" presented to him 18 years later and that mistakes were apparently made.
"If there's a mistake to be made, it would have to be the officer who was responsible for putting those (awards together," he told MSNBC.

CBS reported on Thursday that after questions were raised by veterans, Hackworth removed one of two Distinguished Flying Crosses listed on his home page on the internet and an Army Ranger service tab.

He sent one of the veterans an e-mail message saying he was awarded the Ranger tab "in error" and "I have discovered I only have been awarded one" Distinguished Flying Cross instead of the two he listed, CBS said.
He suggested a "sleepy clerk" at army headquarters made the mistake, and insisted there was a fundamental difference between his case and Boorda's, the network reported.
"I didn't make it up," CBS quoted Hackworth as saying. "Not like Boorda."
